Ambient LLMs:
Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching

Giannis Daras Affiliation: MIT Email: gdaras@mit.edu    Marios Papachristou Affiliation: Arizona State University Email: mpapachr@asu.edu    Adam Klivans Affiliation: University of Texas at Austin Email: klivans@cs.utexas.edu    Antonio Torralba Affiliation: MIT Email: torralba@mit.edu    Constantinos Daskalakis Affiliation: MIT Email: costis@mit.edu
Abstract

Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a “frozen” version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit T→∞T\to\infty reverting back to regular SFT and T=1T=1 to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning.

1 Introduction

The development of state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) has evolved into a complex, multi-stage pipeline (Liu et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2023; Abdin et al., 2024; Achiam et al., 2023; Olmo et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024). This process typically progresses from massive-scale pre-training to more specialized post-training phases, including instruction-tuning (Ouyang et al., 2022), alignment (Ziegler et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2022), and reasoning (Guo et al., 2025; Lightman et al., 2023). As models advance through this pipeline, data availability decreases by orders of magnitude. While pre-training corpora often encompass trillions of tokens, later stages frequently rely on datasets comprising merely a few thousand highly curated examples (Zhou et al., 2023a; Guha et al., 2025). This severe bottleneck arises because post-training requires extraordinarily high-quality data, making large-scale collection prohibitively challenging (Zhou et al., 2023a).

The stark contrast in data scale introduces undesirable artifacts. Most notably, post-trained LLMs tend to suffer from catastrophic forgetting at the tails of the pre-training data distribution, overfitting instead to the specific stylistic patterns or narrow viewpoints overrepresented in the limited post-training data (Ouyang et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2024). This phenomenon is known as the alignment tax (Ouyang et al., 2022). The prevailing solution to this bottleneck is brute force: allocating vast financial and computational resources to scale up the collection of post-training data. In this work, we ask a different question: are there algorithmic solutions that can increase the data efficiency of post-training without inducing severe model collapse or overfitting?

We start our approach to this problem by performing a thought experiment. Imagine having access to an oracle LLM that can generate the high-quality post-training data distribution, but you can only observe a high-temperature, noisy version of its predictions. We show that learning from high-temperature data can match the performance of training on the true, standard-temperature distribution, provided the sample size is large enough. For a practical algorithm, we do not have a perfect high-temperature oracle, but we can effectively approximate it using a high-temperature weak model, which is the model prior to post-training. Distributionally, any two models converge as the sampling temperature increases; thus, at a sufficiently high temperature, a readily available weak model serves as a strong proxy for the unavailable oracle. This motivates our proposed approach: during post-training, we augment our dataset using a weak teacher operating at a high temperature. We enforce that the post-trained model matches the weak teacher’s distribution at this high temperature, while remaining unconstrained to refine its conditional distributions at the standard temperature (T=1T=1). The temperature hyperparameter explicitly controls the level of trust placed in the pre-trained model, with the T→∞T\to\infty limit gracefully reverting to standard SFT and with T=1T=1 to knowledge distillation.

Our algorithm, termed Ambient SFT, mitigates the overfitting typically observed when applying Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to small datasets. It achieves this by adding to the standard SFT loss a second term, which we call Temperature Matching, that regularizes the post-trained network to match the high-temperature conditional distributions of its pre-trained predecessor. We evaluate Ambient SFT across three standard post-training paradigms: (i) domain adaptation, (ii) instruction-tuning, and (iii) the development of reasoning capabilities. Across all settings, our approach consistently outperforms standard SFT. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce Ambient SFT, a drop-in replacement for standard SFT that regularizes fine-tuning by matching a high-temperature version of the model’s own pre-trained distribution. A single temperature knob interpolates between SFT and knowledge distillation.

  • •

    We prove that a target distribution can be recovered from high-temperature conditionals alone, that any two models’ conditionals contract as the temperature grows, and that under a log-linear model Ambient SFT strictly beats vanilla SFT and knowledge distillation.

  • •

    We show gains in all three post-training regimes: up to 26.7%26.7\% lower perplexity than the best baseline across five domain-adaptation targets; average relative gains of 8.0%8.0\% to 20.3%20.3\% on instruction tuning and wins on 5/65/6 reasoning benchmarks.

2 Background

Notation. Let VV be a finite alphabet of tokens, and let L⊆VlL\subseteq V^{l} be a language associated with a probability measure pp. A sample from that language is denoted with 𝐱=(x1,…,xl)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{l}), where xi∈Vx_{i}\in V. We use 𝐱<i=(x1,…,xi−1)\mathbf{x}_{<i}=(x_{1},...,x_{i-1}) to denote the vector with the first (i−1)(i-1) co-ordinates.

Training of Auto-Regressive (AR) Language Models. Any distribution, can be factorized as follows: p⁡(𝐱)=p⁡(x1)​p​(x2|x1)⋅…⋅p⁡(xl|𝐱<l)p(\mathbf{x})=p(x_{1})p(x_{2}|x_{1})\cdot...\cdot p(x_{l}|\mathbf{x}_{<l}). Autoregressive Language Models (LMs) are artificial networks trained to capture these conditional distributions. Specifically, a model gθ(⋅|𝐱<i)g_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}_{<i}) outputs logits for each potential token in the vocabulary given a context 𝐱<i\mathbf{x}_{<i}, inducing conditional distributions:

pθ​(xi∣𝐱<i)=egθ​(xi|𝐱<i)∑yi∈Vegθ​(yi|𝐱<i).\displaystyle p_{\theta}(x_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})=\frac{e^{g_{\theta}(x_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})}}{\sum_{y_{i}\in V}e^{g_{\theta}(y_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})}}. (1)

The standard training objective targets the minimization of the population negative log-likelihood

J⁡(θ)=∑i=1l𝔼𝐱≤i∼p≤i​[−log⁡(egθ​(xi|𝐱<i)∑yi∈Vegθ​(yi|𝐱<i))],J(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{l}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{\leq i}\sim p_{\leq i}}\left[-\log\left(\frac{e^{g_{\theta}(x_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})}}{\sum_{y_{i}\in V}e^{g_{\theta}(y_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})}}\right)\right], (2)

where p≤ip_{\leq i} denotes the distribution of the first ii tokens. Eq. (2) computes the cross-entropy between the model’s predicted distribution and the target distributions of each token xix_{i} observed after its prefix 𝐱<i\mathbf{x}_{<i}. By minimizing this loss, the model approximates the true data conditionals p⁡(xi∣𝐱<i)p(x_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i}).

Adjusting the temperature. At inference time, the sharpness of the learned conditional distributions can be modulated by dividing the network logits by a scalar T>0T>0, known as the sampling temperature. We use pT​θ​(xi|𝐱<i)∝pθ​(xi|𝐱<i)1/Tp_{T\theta}(x_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})\propto p_{\theta}(x_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})^{1/T} to refer to the temperature-scaled distributions:

pT​θ​(xi|𝐱<i)=egθ​(xi|𝐱<i)/T∑yi∈Vegθ​(yi|𝐱<i)/T.p_{T\theta}(x_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})=\frac{e^{g_{\theta}(x_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})/T}}{\sum_{y_{i}\in V}e^{g_{\theta}(y_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})/T}}. (3)

The need for post-training. In practice, we do not have oracle access to the true distribution pp. Instead, we optimize the objective of Eq. (2) using a finite empirical dataset 𝒟p={𝐱(k)}k=1n1\mathcal{D}_{p}=\{\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{n_{1}} sampled from pp. We denote this empirical distribution with p^n1\hat{p}_{n_{1}}. Typically, the success of the generative training depends on the size of n1n_{1}. However, collecting a sufficiently large dataset directly from pp is often prohibitively expensive. For example, pp might represent the distribution of expert-level textbooks or highly specialized instruction-following dialogues. While such in-distribution data is scarce, there exists an abundance of generic text on the web, drawn from a broader, different distribution qq. This necessitates the use of two distinct datasets: a massive dataset 𝒟q={𝐲(k)}k=1n2\mathcal{D}_{q}=\{\mathbf{y}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{n_{2}} sampled from qq, and our limited target dataset 𝒟p\mathcal{D}_{p}, where n1≪n2n_{1}\ll n_{2}. The prevailing learning paradigm leverages both datasets by first pre-training the model on 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} and subsequently fine-tuning it on 𝒟p\mathcal{D}_{p}. Hereafter, we use θpre∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}} and θpost∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}} to denote the parameters of the pre-trained and fine-tuned models.

3 Method and Theoretical Results

Problem setting. In our setting, we assume access to a pre-trained model θpre∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}} but not necessarily to the pre-training dataset 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q}. Our goal is to adapt this model to capture as best as possible the distribution pp, from which we only have access to a small dataset 𝒟p={𝐱(k)}k=1n1\mathcal{D}_{p}=\{\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{n_{1}}.

3.1 Ambient SFT algorithm

We start by presenting our algorithm right away. Ambient SFT fine-tunes a pre-trained model with parameters θpre∗\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*} on the new dataset 𝒟p\mathcal{D}_{p} with two losses on the same tokens: the usual cross-entropy on the observed next token, and a temperature matching loss that pulls the student’s conditional distribution at temperature TT toward the pre-trained model’s conditional distribution at temperature TT. With 𝒟p={𝐱(k)}k=1n1\mathcal{D}_{p}=\{\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{n_{1}} the post-training documents, each of length ll, and pT​θp_{T\theta} the temperature-scaled conditionals of Eq. (3), the objective is

J^λ,T​(θ)=1n1​l​∑k=1n1∑i=1l[−log⁡pθ​(xi(k)∣𝐱<i(k))⏟Clean Cross-entropy+λ​DKL(pT​θpre∗(⋅∣𝐱(k)<i)∥pT​θ(⋅∣𝐱(k)<i))⏟Temperature Matching]\widehat{J}_{\lambda,T}(\theta)=\frac{1}{n_{1}l}\sum_{k=1}^{n_{1}}\sum_{i=1}^{l}\Big[\underbrace{-\log p_{\theta}(x^{(k)}_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}^{(k)}_{<i})}_{\text{Clean Cross-entropy}}+\lambda\underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{T\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}^{(k)}_{<i})\,\|\,p_{T\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}^{(k)}_{<i})\big)}_{\text{Temperature Matching}}\Big] (4)

where the student θ\theta is initialized at θpre∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}}, the teacher θpre∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}} is frozen, and λ>0\lambda>0 sets the relative weight of the two terms. The KL term equals the cross-entropy −∑y∈VpT​θpre∗(y∣𝐱<i(k))logpT​θ(y∣𝐱<i(k))-\sum_{y\in V}p_{T{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}}}}(y\mid\mathbf{x}^{(k)}_{<i})\log p_{T\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{x}^{(k)}_{<i}) up to a constant that does not depend on θ\theta, which is what we optimize.

We refer to the full objective of Eq. (4) as Ambient SFT and to its second term as Temperature Matching. The name connects to Ambient Diffusion (Daras et al., 2023; Daras et al., 2024; Daras et al., 2025; Rodríguez-Muñoz et al., 2026), a line of work that trains diffusion models from corrupted data. Here, we view as corruption the imperfect predictions of the pre-trained teacher, which we only trust at a high TT.

Extreme case 1: T→∞T\to\infty. For any two distributions p,qp,q that have full support, the DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}} distance goes to 00 as T→∞T\to\infty. Hence, the second term disappears, and our method reverts to regular SFT.

Extreme case 2: T=1T=1. On the other hand, setting T=1T=1 gives rise to the classic Knowledge Distillation (KD) loss. Typically, in KD, the student is a weak model, and the teacher is a strong model. In our case, we have the opposite: the teacher is the pre-trained model, and the student is the model being post-trained that is expected to eventually outperform the teacher.

Practical Implementation. Pseudocode is given in Algorithm 1, Appendix B. Our implementation optimizes Eq. (4) stochastically. At every step, with probability pcp_{c} we use the regular SFT loss (clean cross-entropy only). With probability 1−p​c1-pc, we do a forward pass through the frozen teacher and we minimize the Temperature Matching loss between the tempered teacher and tempered student conditionals at every supervised position. In expectation, this implements (4) with λ=(1−pc)/pc\lambda=(1-p_{c})/p_{c}.

Computational overhead. Since Ambient SFT requires an additional forward pass through the frozen teacher, it is more expensive than the regular SFT. Using the standard approximation that a backward pass costs roughly twice a forward pass, the expected per-step compute relative to plain fine-tuning is 1+1−pc3⋅CteacherCstudent1+\frac{1-p_{c}}{3}\cdot\frac{C_{\text{teacher}}}{C_{\text{student}}}, where Cteacher/CstudentC_{\text{teacher}}/C_{\text{student}} is the ratio of teacher to student forward-pass cost. For our Experiments, we typically set pc=0.75p_{c}=0.75 and we use the same model for the student and the teacher. This makes training ≈1.1×\approx 1.1\times slower for the same amount of steps. Hence, Ambient SFT is best suited to settings that are data-limited rather than compute-limited.

Clarification and Related Work. Sometimes in the literature the term KD is used to refer to matching any teacher distribution, independent of the smoothing temperature TT. In fact, Hinton et al. (2015) experiment with matching at different temperatures. The main difference is that we use the pre-trained model to supervise itself during post-training. An algorithm relevant to ours is the one from Li & Hoiem (2017). There a model is adapted to a new task while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of old tasks through regularization toward its own temperature-softened predictions on the previous tasks using new task’s inputs. In LwF the new task has its own output head, so the distillation and new-task losses interact only through shared features. In our work, the output space is shared. This changes the role of temperature that is set to a fixed choice in LwF. In Ambient SFT, the temperature controls a bias-variance trade-off (Theorem 3.2), and it is set based on how much the student trusts the base model. More discussion about related work is presented in Section 5.

3.2 Theoretical Analysis of the Algorithm

We now analyze Ambient SFT theoretically: we show that pure temperature matching is equivalent to learning from high-temperature samples, characterize how fast temperature contracts distributional differences, and establish the statistical benefits of Ambient SFT under a simple log-linear model. Readers interested mainly in the empirical results can skip to Section 4.

3.2.1 Equivalence to learning from high-temperature data

We start by showing that training with the temperature matching loss of Eq. (4) alone is equivalent to learning from high-temperature data alone. The result holds for matching toward any autoregressive model, so we write θ∗\theta^{*} for the teacher; in the algorithm θ∗=θpre∗\theta^{*}=\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}}. The proof is in Appendix E.1.

Theorem 3.1 (Learning from noisy data).

Let pθ∗p_{\theta^{*}} be any AR model over VlV^{l} with logits gθ∗g_{\theta^{*}} as in Eq. (1), and let pT​θ∗(⋅∣𝐱<i)p_{T\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i}) be its temperature-scaled conditionals of Eq. (3). For every position ii, let μi\mu_{i} be any distribution over prefixes 𝐱<i∈Vi−1\mathbf{x}_{<i}\in V^{i-1}.

  1. (a)

    Temperature Matching is equivalent to learning from high-temperature samples. Let RT(θ)=∑i=1l𝔼𝐱<i∼μi[DKL(pT​θ∗(⋅∣𝐱<i)∥pT​θ(⋅∣𝐱<i))]R_{T}(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{l}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{<i}\sim\mu_{i}}\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{T\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})\,\|\,p_{T\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})\big)\big] be the (population-level) temperature-matching loss of Eq. (4) with teacher θ∗\theta^{*}, and let

    JT(θ)=∑i=1l𝔼𝐱<i∼μi𝔼xi∼pT​θ∗(⋅∣𝐱<i)[−logpT​θ(xi∣𝐱<i)]\displaystyle J_{T}(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{l}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{<i}\sim\mu_{i}}\,\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim p_{T\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})}\left[-\log p_{T\theta}(x_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})\right] (5)

    be the cross-entropy on next tokens sampled at temperature TT. Then JTJ_{T}, RTR_{T} have the same minimizers. Unlike RTR_{T}, JTJ_{T} needs only samples from the tempered model, not its logits.

  2. (b)

    Exact recovery at any finite TT. If θ\theta minimizes JTJ_{T} at any T>0T>0, then pT′​θ(⋅∣𝐱<i)=pT′​θ∗(⋅∣𝐱<i)p_{T^{\prime}\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})=p_{T^{\prime}\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i}) for every context 𝐱<i\mathbf{x}_{<i} in the support of μi\mu_{i} and every T′>0T^{\prime}>0, i.e., matching the teacher at any temperature implies matching the teacher at all temperatures. Moreover, this implies that gθ(⋅∣𝐱<i)=gθ∗(⋅∣𝐱<i)+c(𝐱<i)g_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})=g_{\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})+c(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) for a context-dependent constant. The prefix distributions only decide on which contexts the teacher is matched.

Prefixes sampled from the tempered teacher are a special case (Corollary E.1, Appendix E.1); in Eq. (4), the prefixes come from the fine-tuning data. The theorem shows that the distribution is identifiable from high-temperature data. This is perhaps counterintuitive: at high TT, samples look gibberish. Yet they still carry a learning signal, and a model trained with Eq. (12) recovers the distribution, producing reasonable samples as shown in Figure 2(a).

3.2.2 Temperature scaling as a contraction mechanism

If we had lots of data from pθpost∗p_{\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}, we could run temperature matching towards it for any TT of our choice. Unfortunately, in our setting we assume we do not have many data from it. What happens if we run temperature matching to the weak teacher pθpre∗p_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}} instead? The following result establishes an upper bound on the KL divergence between the two distributions, for any fixed context as the temperature TT increases. We show that, for every context 𝐱<i\mathbf{x}_{<i} and every T>0T>0:

DKL(pT​θpost∗(⋅∣𝐱<i)∥pT​θpre∗(⋅∣𝐱<i))≤Δ​(𝐱<i)28​T2,\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})\,\middle\|\,p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})\right)\leq\frac{\Delta(\mathbf{x}_{<i})^{2}}{8T^{2}}, (6)

where Δ⁡(𝐱<i)\Delta(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) is the range over y∈Vy\in V of the logit gap gθpost∗​(y∣𝐱<i)−gθpre∗​(y∣𝐱<i)g_{\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})-g_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i}). Our bound is stated in more detail in Appendix E.2. The bound gives a rate of O⁡(T−2)O(T^{-2}) for every context.

3.2.3 Ambient SFT analysis under a log-linear model

We are now ready to put all the pieces together. Theorem 3.1 establishes the equivalence of Temperature Matching to learning from corrupted data from the teacher and shows that for any finite TT, the teacher distribution is the minimizer of this term alone. Training with Temperature Matching alone would be problematic since we would not be able to move from the pre-training distribution. Our algorithm trains with both regular SFT and Temperature Matching, with a choice of temperature TT controlling the level at which the gradients from the weak teacher can be reliable, as quantified by Eq. (6). The questions left to answer are: (a) what is the right choice of temperature in the temperature matching term, and (b) for the optimal amount of temperature, do we get any statistical advantage compared to learning from regular SFT alone? In what follows, we answer those questions. To avoid arguing about how LLMs generalize to new contexts not seen in training, we adopt a simple log-linear next-token model with frozen features, and analyze (4) on it exactly.

A log-linear model. Let ϕ:V→ℝd\phi:V\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a fixed token embedding and ψ:V∗→ℝm\psi:V^{*}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} a fixed context representation (e.g., the pre-trained network’s last hidden state). Assume both functions have bounded ℓ2\ell_{2} norms. The learnable parameter θ\theta is a single matrix, which we will also denote Aθ∈ℝd×mA_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}, and

pθ​(y∣𝐱<i)=exp⁡(ϕ​(y)⊤​Aθ​ψ​(𝐱<i))∑z∈Vexp⁡(ϕ​(z)⊤​Aθ​ψ​(𝐱<i))p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})=\frac{\exp\big(\phi(y)^{\top}A_{\theta}\psi(\mathbf{x}_{<i})\big)}{\sum_{z\in V}\exp\big(\phi(z)^{\top}A_{\theta}\psi(\mathbf{x}_{<i})\big)} (7)

Write Λ(η)=log∑z∈Vexp(ϕ(z)⊤η)\Lambda(\eta)=\log\sum_{z\in V}\exp(\phi(z)^{\top}\eta) for the log-normalizer of (7), i.e. the logarithm of its denominator, and μ⁡(η)=∇Λ​(η)=𝔼pη​[ϕ⁡(y)]\mu(\eta)=\nabla\Lambda(\eta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\eta}}[\phi(y)], Σ⁡(η)=∇2Λ​(η)=Covpη⁡[ϕ⁡(y)]\Sigma(\eta)=\nabla^{2}\Lambda(\eta)=\operatorname{Cov}_{p_{\eta}}[\phi(y)] for the mean embedding and the covariance of the conditional with natural parameter η=Aθ​ψ​(𝐱<i)\eta=A_{\theta}\psi(\mathbf{x}_{<i}). Flattening the sum of (4), the n1n_{1} documents supply n=n1​ln=n_{1}l token observations (𝐱<t,xt)(\mathbf{x}_{<t},x_{t}), t=1,…,nt=1,\ldots,n, and we write ψt=ψ⁡(𝐱<t)\psi_{t}=\psi(\mathbf{x}_{<t}). We will use θ\theta and AθA_{\theta} interchangeably.

The objective. Instantiating (4) on this model, gives, up to additive constants that do not depend on θ\theta,

J^λ,T​(θ)=1n​∑t=1n[Λ⁡(Aθ​ψt)−ϕ​(xt)⊤​Aθ​ψt]⏟L^​(θ)​(clean cross-entropy)+λ​1n​∑t=1n[Λ⁡(Aθ​ψtT)−μ​(Aθpre∗​ψtT)⊤​Aθ​ψtT]⏟R^T​(θ)​(temperature matching).\widehat{J}_{\lambda,T}(\theta)=\underbrace{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\Big[\Lambda(A_{\theta}\psi_{t})-\phi(x_{t})^{\top}A_{\theta}\psi_{t}\Big]}_{\widehat{L}(\theta)\ \text{(clean cross-entropy)}}\;+\;\lambda\,\underbrace{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\Big[\Lambda\!\big(\tfrac{A_{\theta}\psi_{t}}{T}\big)-\mu\!\big(\tfrac{A_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}\psi_{t}}{T}\big)^{\!\top}\tfrac{A_{\theta}\psi_{t}}{T}\Big]}_{\widehat{R}_{T}(\theta)\ \text{(temperature matching)}}. (8)

Write θ^λ\widehat{\theta}_{\lambda} for the minimizer of (8). Our goal in this section is to bound its distance from θpost∗\theta_{\rm post}^{*} and study the benefit of including temperature matching term in the objective.

Remark: For simplicity, we assume below that, in the data (𝐱<t,xt)(\mathbf{x}_{<t},x_{t}), t=1,…,nt=1,\ldots,n, that we have available for training, the prefixes 𝐱<t\mathbf{x}_{<t} are drawn i.i.d. from pθpost∗p_{\theta^{*}_{\rm post}} and the tokens xtx_{t} are also drawn independently from each other from pθpost∗(⋅|𝐱<t)p_{\theta^{*}_{\rm post}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}_{<t}). We denote with 𝒟x\mathcal{D}_{x} the distribution of prefixes drawn from pθpost∗p_{\theta^{*}_{\rm post}}. Appendix E.3 discusses how to deal with dependencies of tokens in documents.

Three quantities govern our result, where all expectations below are with respect to prefixes 𝐱<t∼𝒟x\mathbf{x}_{<t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{x}, ψ=ψ⁡(𝐱<t)\psi=\psi(\mathbf{x}_{<t}), and ⊗\otimes is the Kronecker product:

F=𝔼⁡[Σ⁡(Aθpost∗​ψ)⊗ψ​ψ⊤],HT=1T2​𝔼​[Σ⁡(Aθpost∗​ψT)⊗ψ​ψ⊤],B=Aθpost∗−Aθpre∗.F=\mathbb{E}\big[\Sigma(A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}\psi)\otimes\psi\psi^{\top}\big],\quad H_{T}=\frac{1}{T^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\Sigma(\tfrac{A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}\psi}{T})\otimes\psi\psi^{\top}\big],\quad B=A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}-A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}}}.

We assume throughout that the frozen features are non-degenerate: G=𝔼⁡[ψ​ψ⊤]≻0G=\mathbb{E}[\psi\psi^{\top}]\succ 0, and the embedding differences ϕ⁡(y)−ϕ⁡(z)\phi(y)-\phi(z) span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. The latter fails only if some v≠0v\neq 0 has ϕ​(y)⊤​v\phi(y)^{\top}v constant in yy, in which case AθA_{\theta} would not be identifiable; under the two conditions FF and HTH_{T} are positive definite, so the inverses below are literal and ‖Aθ^−Aθpost∗‖F\|A_{\widehat{\theta}}-A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}\|_{F} is a well-defined risk.

FF is the Fisher information matrix controlling the curvature of the first term in the loss function. It measures how much the target data tell us about each direction of Aθpost∗A_{\theta_{\rm post}^{*}}.

HTH_{T} is the curvature of the temperature matching penalty term. As TT grows the tempered conditional approaches uniform, so Σ⁡(Aθ​ψ/T)→Σ0:=Covunif⁡(V)⁡[ϕ⁡(y)]\Sigma(A_{\theta}\psi/T)\to\Sigma_{0}:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathrm{unif}(V)}[\phi(y)] for every θ\theta and HT≈Σ0⊗G/T2H_{T}\approx\Sigma_{0}\otimes G/T^{2}, where G=𝔼⁡[ψ​ψ⊤]G=\mathbb{E}[\psi\psi^{\top}], which is the same context geometry as FF, but with a token covariance that never degenerates. The teacher thus adds curvature precisely where the data supplies none.

The next theorem quantifies how these quantities affect the estimation error. The expansion concerns the regime in which the teacher’s error and the statistical error of maximum likelihood are comparable, both of order n−1/2n^{-1/2}, which is where the tradeoff between them is nontrivial. We therefore state the result under ∥B∥=O(n−1/2)\|B\|=O(n^{-1/2}). The proof is in Appendix E.3.

Theorem 3.2 (Risk expansion and generic improvement over T=1T=1).

Suppose ∥B∥=O(n−1/2)\|B\|=O(n^{-1/2}). Then

𝔼​‖Aθ^λ,T−Aθpost∗‖F2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big\|A_{\widehat{\theta}_{\lambda,T}}-A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}\big\|_{F}^{2} =ρ(λ,T)+O(n−3/2),\displaystyle=\rho(\lambda,T)+O(n^{-3/2}),
ρ⁡(λ,T)\displaystyle\rho(\lambda,T) =λ2​‖(F+λ​HT)−1​HT​B‖F2⏟bias2+1n​tr⁡((F+λ​HT)−1​F​(F+λ​HT)−1)⏟variance,\displaystyle=\underbrace{\lambda^{2}\|(F+\lambda H_{T})^{-1}H_{T}B\|_{F}^{2}}_{\text{bias}^{2}}+\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{n}\operatorname{tr}\!\big((F+\lambda H_{T})^{-1}F(F+\lambda H_{T})^{-1}\big)}_{\text{variance}}, (9)

uniformly for λ\lambda and TT in a fixed range bounded away from 00 and ∞\infty. Moreover, interior choices of (λ,T)(\lambda,T) do at least as well as all three extremes:

inf0<λ<∞0<T<∞,T≠1ρ⁡(λ,T)≤min⁡{tr⁡(F−1)/n⏟maximum likelihood,‖B‖F2⏟frozen teacher,minλ⁡ρ⁡(λ,1)⏟knowledge distillation},\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}0<\lambda<\infty\\ 0<T<\infty,\ T\neq 1\end{subarray}}\rho(\lambda,T)\ \leq\ \min\Big\{\underbrace{\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1})/n}_{\text{maximum likelihood}},\ \underbrace{\|B\|_{F}^{2}}_{\text{frozen teacher}},\ \underbrace{\textstyle\min_{\lambda}\rho(\lambda,1)}_{\text{knowledge distillation}}\Big\}, (10)

Under a mild non-degeneracy condition, and for every BB outside a closed Lebesgue-null cone (see Appendix E.3), the inequality is strict: some finite (λ,T)(\lambda,T) with T≠1T\neq 1 strictly beats all three.

4 Experiments

4.1 Learning from high-temperature data

We first verify that training on high-temperature samples can still recover the original (T=1T=1) distribution. We train a model on a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, sample from it at temperature TT to obtain 𝒟T′\mathcal{D}_{T}^{\prime}, train a new model on 𝒟T′\mathcal{D}_{T}^{\prime} with Eq. (12), and measure its perplexity on a clean validation set.

For our first toy experiment, we use a GPT-2 architecture, and we train it on the tiny Shakespeare dataset (Karpathy, 2015). Figure 2(b) shows the validation perplexity of a model trained with the objective of Eq. (12) and a baseline trained with the normal loss function of Eq. (2) for different temperatures. As shown, our algorithm achieves relatively low validation perplexity with respect to the clean distribution even for high training corruption strengths. We proceed to repeat the idea at a larger scale. We train a GPT-2 124M model on OpenWebText (≈9\approx 9B tokens), and we use it to produce synthetic data at different temperatures as before. Figure 2(a) shows examples of training and generated data. The model is capable of producing clean samples even though it has only been trained with text that appears gibberish. These experiments validate that the high-temperature distributions still have usable learning signal, despite the seemingly uninformative training data. Theorem 3.1 establishes that Temperature Matching is exactly equivalent to learning from corrupted samples.

4.2 Domain Adaptation Experiments

We proceed to post-training experiments, beginning with domain adaptation: a model pre-trained on generic text needs to be adapted to a new domain from which we don’t have much data. We start with an 1.51.5B-parameter model pre-trained on OpenWebText. We adapt to five target domains, chosen to span diverse text types: Python code (CodeParrot Team, 2022; Chen et al., 2021)), CS papers (Lo et al., 2020), biomedical text (Stuhlmann et al., 2025), news (Hamborg et al., 2017), and product reviews (Hou et al., 2026), each using ≈\approx225M tokens. We benchmark: (a) training from scratch on the domain of interest, (b) fine-tuning, (c) data-mixing (where we split training updates between the pre-training domain and the target domain), (d) our Ambient SFT approach. We always pick the hyperparameters that achieve the lowest validation perplexity in the target domain. Our algorithm has two hyperparameters pcp_{c}, which controls how often we apply the Temperature Matching loss and the temperature TT. We give a full sweep of these parameters in Appendix C.1.2.

We report results in Table 1. As shown, Ambient SFT matches or outperforms prior baselines across all five domains. For News, the relative improvement in perplexity over the best baseline reaches 26.7%26.7\%; in validation loss, this is a reduction from 1.991.99 to 1.681.68.

Predicting the success of Ambient SFT. The benefit varies across domains: it is largest on Python Code and News and smaller elsewhere. Because success depends on how much the teacher knows about the target domain, a cheap and reliable predictor of the benefit is the model’s perplexity on the target domain before fine-tuning. Across the five domains, this heuristic gives a Spearman rank correlation of ρ=−0.90\rho=-0.90 between zero-shot loss and win margin to the baselines. This is qualitatively consistent with Theorem 3.2, whose bias term depends on the discrepancy B=Aθpost∗−Aθpre∗B=A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}-A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}}}. Full per-domain zero-shot loss and win-margin numbers are reported in Table 19.

Effect of temperature TT. The Temperature Matching term disappears as T→∞T\to\infty, and it becomes KD for T=1T=1. Figure 3(a) sweeps TT, holding every other setting fixed. Neither extreme is optimal: validation loss falls steadily from T=1T=1 down to a minimum at T=2.5T=2.5, then rises and plateaus. Beyond this ablation, we clarify that we got the optimal pcp_{c} and TT values used in Table 1 by optimizing over the joint parameter space. Hence, the optimal temperature T∗T^{*} satisfies T∗≠1T^{*}\neq 1.

Effect of the size of the student and teacher. In our experiments so far, the teacher is the frozen model after pre-training and the student is initialized from this teacher. Table 21 isolates the effect of student and teacher capacity, testing four combinations of student size (124M, 1.5B) and teacher size (124M, 1.5B). Two trends are unsurprising: (a) a larger student improves results at both teacher sizes, and (b) a larger teacher improves results at both student sizes. A third, less obvious finding is that a small (124M) teacher can still improve a strictly larger (1.5B) student, a pairing that classical KD would not predict to help. Pairing the 1.5B student with the 124M teacher beats plain fine-tuning of the same 1.5B student with no teacher at all on Python Code and News.

Effect of number of tokens of the target domain. To understand the effect of the size of the fine-tuning dataset, we subsample the Python Code training set, keeping only 1/31/3 and 1/101/10, and finetune a 124M model on each subsampled set with both Ambient SFT and the Data Mixture baseline. Figure 3(b) reports the results: our method consistently outperforms the baseline, and the gap widens as the dataset shrinks. This is intuitive: with enough target-domain data, our method should not help, but it is highly effective when data, not compute, is the bottleneck. This matches Theorem 3.2: the bias term is independent of nn, while the sampling-variance term is not.

4.3 Instruction-tuning experiments

Having established Ambient SFT as a drop-in replacement for SFT in domain adaptation, we now ask whether it helps elsewhere in the post-training stack, starting with instruction tuning, where a pre-trained LLM is trained via SFT to follow instructions. We start with pre-trained base models, ranging from 1.71.7B to 1414B params, and we fine-tune them on the Dolci-Instruct-SFT (Olmo et al., 2025). We start our evaluation by using only ≈20\approx 20K documents (≈18\approx 18M tokens). We validate performance on standard benchmarks that measure instruction following (IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023b)), knowledge (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017)), math (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021)), code (HumanEval+ (Chen et al., 2021)), and general reasoning (BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023)). For all our runs, we use pc=0.75p_{c}=0.75 (i.e., 25%25\% of the updates are spent on the Temperature Matching term) and T=2.5T=2.5.

Results are presented in Table 2, where we show results for Qwen3 models ranging from 1.7B to 14B parameters. We start by analyzing what Vanilla SFT does to the capabilities of the underlying model. As shown, Vanilla SFT improves instruction-following capabilities by a lot (e.g. IFEval increases from 45.5%45.5\% to 76.3%76.3\% at the 4B scale) but leads to catastrophic forgetting on the rest of the benchmarks: the base model (pre-SFT) beats vanilla-SFT on 6 or 7 tasks for every model. On the contrary, Ambient SFT leads to consistent average improvements ranging from 8.0%8.0\% to 20.3%20.3\%. At every size and model family, Ambient SFT matches or beats vanilla SFT on every benchmark except IFEval, and significantly outperforms the base model on IFEval. Beyond that, Ambient SFT mostly preserves knowledge (MMLU, PopQA, TriviaQA), and increases capabilities in math: it is above the base model on both GSM8K and MATH for almost every model tested.

Effect of model size. The gain is largest at the smallest scale but persists as models grow: the average relative improvement is +20.3%+20.3\% at 1.7B and stays above +8.0%+8.0\% from 4B to 14B. On the eight-benchmark average, Ambient SFT at 8B equals vanilla SFT at 14B, and on MATH Ambient SFT at 1.7B already exceeds vanilla SFT at 8B. At 14B, Ambient SFT ties Vanilla SFT on IFEval.

Per-source temperature. The only benchmark where Ambient SFT is worse than vanilla SFT is IFEval. We find the problem originates from the composition of our dataset. Dolci-Instruct-SFT mixes 21 sources, and the base model fits some of them much better than others. Setting the temperature separately for each source improves IFEval at every model size, while keeping other gains. Results are shown in Table 3 and details on how to set the temperature for each source are given in Appendix D.5.

Generalization to other model families. Table 4 shows more model families for which Ambient SFT outperforms vanilla SFT. Specifically, we show large gains for OLMo-3-7B and Llama-3.1-8B.

Effect of dataset size. We now study what happens when we use 1%,10%1\%,10\% and 100%100\% of the dataset. The greatest improvements are observed in the 1%1\% of the dataset setting, as expected, with an average 15.4%15.4\% relative improvement over vanilla SFT; with 10%10\% of the dataset, the average relative improvement is 3.4%3.4\%. That said, even at full data scale, Ambient SFT leads to an average 8.6%8.6\% relative improvement to vanilla SFT. Figure 6 shows per-benchmark scores across different scales.

Ambient SFT reduces overfitting. We hypothesize that Ambient SFT reduces overfitting, letting the model benefit from more epochs than vanilla SFT. To test this, we train for 22, 44, 66, 88, and 1010 epochs on a 10%10\% subset of Dolci-Instruct-SFT (215k examples). As Figure 4 shows, Ambient SFT reaches its best performance at more epochs and is more robust to overfitting.

Vanilla SFT trades knowledge for instruction following. For vanilla SFT, the number of epochs controls a trade-off. Going from 22 to 66 epochs raises IFEval from 71.071.0 to 80.880.8, but lowers every other benchmark: MATH from 37.337.3 to 30.030.0, GSM8K from 76.476.4 to 69.669.6, HumanEval+ from 81.381.3 to 75.575.5, MMLU from 66.366.3 to 65.065.0, PopQA from 19.419.4 to 17.217.2, TriviaQA from 63.763.7 to 59.259.2 and BBH from 62.862.8 to 58.958.9. Stopping early therefore limits forgetting only by giving up instruction following. Ambient SFT does not face this trade-off: over the same range, IFEval rises from 63.863.8 to 73.473.4, while the other benchmarks stay within about two points of their 2-epoch values.

Comparison with other regularizers. Our Temperature Matching term can be thought as regularization. To compare with other regularizers, Table 5 shows results on Qwen3-1.7B with L2-SP (Li et al., 2018), NEFTune (Jain et al., 2024), KD toward the frozen base model at T=1T=1, and label smoothing, each at its best setting. Ambient SFT outperforms other regularization methods. It reaches +20.3%+20.3\% over vanilla SFT, with the second best method being KD (Ambient SFT with T=1T=1) with +17.0%+17.0\%.

4.4 Reasoning experiments

Finally, we test whether Ambient SFT benefits reasoning. We train OLMo-3-7B on ≈22\approx 22K examples (1%1\%) of Dolci-Think-SFT (Olmo et al., 2025) with the same hyperparameters as before. We evaluate on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), AIME 2024 and 2025, HumanEval+ (Chen et al., 2021), IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023b), and GPQA (Rein et al., 2023) (details in Appendix C.3.1). As Table 6 shows, Ambient SFT outperforms vanilla SFT on 5/6 benchmarks and trails by only 1.21.2 points on GSM8K. While there is a consistent boost in reasoning abilities, its magnitude is smaller compared to the one observed for domain adaptation and instruction-tuning. That said, Table 23 further shows that reasoning models trained with Ambient SFT are also more robust to prompting than pure SFT ones. Ambient SFT also is the only regularization method that leads to improvements over SFT for reasoning, as both KD and L2-SP lead to regression in the reasoning scores.

5 Related Work

Our work builds upon the Knowledge Distillation (KD) literature pioneered by Buciluǎ et al. (2006) and Hinton et al. (2015). In the context of LLMs, KD has been successfully applied in the works of (Kim & Rush, 2016; Gu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019). However, whereas classical KD employs a teacher that is stronger or more aligned than the student, our framework inverts this dynamic: the teacher model is strictly weaker at the target task. Because the student (the fine-tuned model) is expected to outperform the teacher (the frozen pre-trained model), the teacher’s role is not to act as an oracle. Instead, it serves to regularize the fine-tuning process by providing coarse, high-temperature supervision. We also note that applying KD on smoothed distributions has been explored in the paper by (Hinton et al., 2015) and an explicit scaling term 1/T21/T^{2} has been proposed. In our experiments, we do not find this scaling to be optimal across all of our settings, and we apply Knowledge Distillation to a previous version of the same model instead of an external more powerful teacher. The concept of self-distillation has also been explored in (Yang et al., 2024). The main difference between this work and ours is that we match towards the full high-temperature distribution of the teacher, while the authors of (Yang et al., 2024) run SFT over datasets produced by the model.

Closer to our setting is the continual-learning literature on avoiding catastrophic forgetting without access to the original training data. Li & Hoiem (2017) propose recording the pre-update network’s outputs on the new task’s own inputs and adds a temperature-softened distillation term to the new task’s loss, anchoring the update to the model’s previous behavior without replaying old data. Our method shares that structure: the frozen pre-trained model is queried on the fine-tuning data itself, and the match is enforced after raising the temperature.

The concept of anchoring a model to a prior state also frequently appears in reinforcement learning (RL) alignment pipelines, where a KL-divergence penalty against a reference model is used to prevent reward hacking (Ouyang et al., 2022). Our framework diverges from this paradigm in two critical ways. First, our method targets the Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stage rather than the RL phase. Second, we exclusively match the high-temperature distributions of the reference model. Enforcing a strict match at T=1T=1 would actively degrade performance by forcing the student to adopt the unaligned base model’s lack of task awareness, a manifestation of the phenomenon known as alignment tax (Ouyang et al., 2022). By matching the reference model only at a coarse level, our method successfully avoids this tax while maintaining structural regularization. Table 7 in Appendix A summarizes how Ambient SFT differs from these techniques.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

We introduced Ambient SFT, a drop-in replacement for SFT that adds to the standard cross-entropy loss a term matching the model to a high-temperature version of its own pre-trained predictions. Across domain adaptation, instruction tuning, and reasoning, Ambient SFT outperforms vanilla SFT, with the largest gains when fine-tuning data are scarce. A natural next step is to extend this anchoring idea beyond SFT to the reinforcement-learning algorithms used in post-training.

Appendix A Comparison with Prior Techniques

Appendix B Training Algorithm

Algorithm 1 is the stochastic implementation of the objective (4) of Section 3.1. Each step draws one rank-synchronized coin: with probability pcp_{c} the batch takes a standard SFT step, and otherwise the frozen teacher is run forward without gradients and the step minimizes the matching loss at every supervised position. In expectation this is (4) with λ=(1−pc)/pc\lambda=(1-p_{c})/p_{c}, and pc=1p_{c}=1 recovers SFT exactly.

Appendix C Experimental Details

C.1 Domain Adaptation

C.1.1 Datasets

All models are pre-trained on OpenWebText (≈\approx9B tokens), a publicly available reproduction of the WebText corpus used to train GPT-2, obtained from the Skylion007/openwebtext11 1 https://huggingface.co/datasets/Skylion007/openwebtext Hugging Face dataset. For the domain adaptation experiments of Section 4.2, we adapt these pre-trained models to five target domains, chosen to span a diverse range of text types. Each domain corpus is capped at ≈\approx225M target-domain tokens, matching the same order of magnitude across domains so that no single domain benefits from a systematically larger fine-tuning set. The domains, their sources, and the exact Hugging Face datasets used are:

  • •

    Python Code: an ≈225\approx 225M token subset of the CodeParrot clean-train dataset (CodeParrot Team, 2022), itself built from permissively-licensed GitHub Python repositories in the style of the training corpus used by Chen et al. (2021). codeparrot/codeparrot-clean-train22 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/codeparrot/codeparrot-clean-train.

  • •

    CS: computer science paper abstracts drawn from S2ORC, the Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (Lo et al., 2020). AlgorithmicResearchGroup/s2orc-cs-enriched33 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/AlgorithmicResearchGroup/s2orc-cs-enriched.

  • •

    BioMed: biomedical abstracts drawn from PubMed metadata (National Library of Medicine), via the subset released alongside Stuhlmann et al. (2025). slinusc/PubMedAbstractsSubset44 4 https://huggingface.co/datasets/slinusc/PubMedAbstractsSubset.

  • •

    News: English-language news articles from CC-News, a Common Crawl news dataset extracted with the news-please crawler (Hamborg et al., 2017). vblagoje/cc_news55 5 https://huggingface.co/datasets/vblagoje/cc_news.

  • •

    Reviews: Amazon product reviews (books category), drawn from the Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset (Hou et al., 2026). cogsci13/Amazon-Reviews-2023-Books-Review66 6 huggingface.co/datasets/cogsci13/Amazon-Reviews-2023-Books-Review.

C.1.2 Full (p,T)(p,T) sweep and optimal hyperparameters

Table 13 reports the optimal (p,T)(p,T) per domain used to produce Table 20 and Table 21’s 124M-student rows. The optimal mixing ratio pp was 0.50.5 in every one of the 10 cells tested, so the table reports only TT.

For the Small Teacher condition specifically, Tables 8–12 report the full (p,T)(p,T) grid each domain’s optimum was selected from: a uniform 15-point grid (p∈{0.5,0.75,0.9}×T∈{1.25,1.5,1.75,2.0,2.5}p\in\{0.5,0.75,0.9\}\times T\in\{1.25,1.5,1.75,2.0,2.5\}) for CS, BioMed, News, and Reviews, and a wider grid for Python Code.

Table 14 reports the analogous optimal (p,T)(p,T) for the 1.5B student, Ambient SFT’s self-teacher condition (Table 1 and Table 21’s “1.5B & 1.5B (self)” row) – the only 1.5B-student condition that received a real per-domain (p,T)(p,T) search in this work. Unlike the 124M student, the optimal pp is not uniform across domains, so both pp and TT are reported. We do not report an analogous table for the 1.5B student paired with the 124M teacher (Table 21’s “1.5B & 124M” row): that condition reuses the (p,T)(p,T) found optimal at the 124M-student scale rather than being independently retuned, so there is no separate search to report.

C.2 Instruction Tuning

C.2.1 Training hyperparameters

Every instruction-tuning run in this paper uses the same training recipe, listed in Table 15; vanilla SFT and Ambient SFT differ only in the loss. Runs are trained with the OLMo-core trainer, starting from each model’s released base checkpoint. The recipe follows Ai2’s instruction-tuning recipe for OLMo 3 (learning rate, schedule, batch size and sequence length) and is kept fixed across base models and model sizes; we did not tune it per model. The one exception is Llama-3.1-8B (Table 4), for which both vanilla SFT and Ambient SFT use a peak learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}. The only settings that change between experiments are the number of epochs (Table 16) and the tokenizer, which is each base model’s own. Every run uses 16 GH200 GPUs; the global batch is fixed in tokens, so the gradient-accumulation factor absorbs the context-parallel degree.

C.2.2 Evaluation harness

All instruction-tuning results (Tables 2, 4 and Figure 4) come from a single, fixed evaluation setup, applied identically to every checkpoint. We use the olmes evaluation suite (Gu et al., 2024) (github.com/allenai/olmes, commit 5a51f502, unmodified) with the vLLM backend (vLLM 0.13.0, PyTorch 2.9.0, Transformers 4.57.6, Python 3.11). Trained checkpoints are converted to the Hugging Face format and evaluated with the chat template stored alongside them: the OLMo 3 instruct template (<|im_start|>/<|im_end|> turns with its default system prompt), which is also the template used to format the training data, for all three base models. Every checkpoint is evaluated once per task, with no selection over seeds or decoding settings.

Table 17 lists the eight task specifications. “Chat” tasks format each prompt (including the few-shot examples, as earlier turns) with the chat template; “plain” tasks feed a raw text prompt. The reported score is the task’s primary metric; for MMLU, MATH and BBH it is the unweighted mean over their subjects or subtasks. The relative change reported in the last column of the instruction-tuning tables is the mean over the eight tasks of (score−scoreSFT)/scoreSFT(\text{score}-\text{score}_{\text{SFT}})/\text{score}_{\text{SFT}}.

Commands. The environment and the evaluation of one checkpoint $CKPT (a Hugging Face model directory) are:

git clone https://github.com/allenai/olmes.git && cd olmes
git checkout 5a51f502d463b8cdc4a2dcad7d7096c41ff1197e
pip install -e . && pip install vllm==0.13.0

export VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn
MARGS="gpu_memory_utilization=0.85,max_length=32768"
MARGS="$MARGS,trust_remote_code=false,add_bos_token=false"
TASKS="ifeval::tulu mmlu::olmes gsm8k::olmes codex_humanevalplus::tulu"
TASKS="$TASKS minerva_math::tulu popqa::tulu"
TASKS="$TASKS triviaqa::olmes bbh:cot::olmes"
for TASK in $TASKS; do
  olmes --model-type vllm --model "$CKPT" --model-args "$MARGS" \
        --task "$TASK" --output-dir "$OUT/$(echo $TASK | tr ’:/’ ’__’)"
done

For Llama-3.1-8B we set add_bos_token=true: olmes encodes prompts without special tokens, and a Llama model trained with a beginning-of-sequence token on every document produces degenerate output without it.

Sharding. To finish each evaluation in minutes rather than hours, we split every task’s instances into 16 disjoint shards and run the command above on each shard in parallel, one GPU per shard. Per-subtask scores are combined across shards weighted by instance count, and the subject and subtask means are taken afterwards, which reproduces the aggregation of an unsharded run.

C.3 Reasoning

C.3.1 Evaluation harness

Reasoning (“Think”) checkpoints are evaluated with the same software as Appendix C.2.2 (olmes commit 5a51f502, vLLM 0.13.0) but with the olmo3:adapt task specifications, the ones behind Ai2’s OLMo 3 Think model card. Every task is zero-shot and chat-formatted with the OLMo 3 Think chat template, whose generation prompt ends with <|im_start|>assistant\n<think>, so every response starts inside a reasoning block and the model must close it with </think> before its final answer. All generation is sampled with temperature 0.6 and top-pp 0.95. The model context is capped at 32,768 tokens (prompt plus response); AIME additionally caps the response at 16,384 tokens. Table 18 lists the six tasks.

Commands. With the environment of Appendix C.2.2, one Think checkpoint $CKPT is evaluated with:

export VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn
MARGS="gpu_memory_utilization=0.85,max_length=32768"
MARGS="$MARGS,trust_remote_code=false,add_bos_token=false"
TASKS="gsm8k::olmo3:adapt aime:2024::olmo3:adapt aime:2025::olmo3:adapt"
TASKS="$TASKS ifeval::olmo3:adapt codex_humanevalplus::olmo3:adapt"
TASKS="$TASKS gpqa::olmo3:adapt"
for TASK in $TASKS; do
  olmes --model-type vllm --model "$CKPT" --model-args "$MARGS" \
        --task "$TASK" --output-dir "$OUT/$(echo $TASK | tr ’:/’ ’__’)"
done

The same 16-way sharding and instance-weighted aggregation as in Appendix C.2.2 are used. Because generation is sampled, repeated evaluations of the same checkpoint differ slightly; AIME’s 32 samples per problem keep the sampling standard error of its score at about one point (0.8 to 1.2 points for the checkpoints in this paper).

Appendix D Additional Results

D.1 Full temperature sweep on Tiny Shakespeare

Figure 2(b) shows the T≥1T\geq 1 half of the sweep, the regime the method operates in. Figure 5 adds the low-temperature half, which is symmetric: sampling far below T=1T=1 is also a corruption, producing repetitive rather than random text, and the objective of Eq. (12) again tracks clean-data training over a much wider range of TT than standard cross-entropy does.

D.2 Domain Adaptation

D.2.1 Predicting the success of Ambient SFT

Table 19 reports the zero-shot validation loss of the pre-trained (1.5B) model on each target domain, before any fine-tuning, alongside Ambient SFT’s win margin over the best baseline from Table 1, as discussed in Section 4.2.

D.2.2 Ablation: effect of a smaller student

Table 20 repeats the domain-adaptation comparison of Table 1 with a 124M-parameter student in place of the 1.5B one, holding every other condition fixed (same target domains, same OWT-pretrained 1.5B teacher for Ambient SFT). Ambient SFT (Small Teacher) additionally reports a self-teacher variant, where the frozen teacher is the same 124M OWT-pretrained checkpoint as the student’s own initialization, rather than the larger 1.5B model. Comparing against Table 1 isolates the effect of student capacity: every resume-based method improves substantially with the larger student, and Ambient SFT’s margin over the baselines is preserved across the scale change.

D.2.3 Ablation: effect of a weaker teacher

Table 21 isolates the effect of teacher strength on Ambient SFT, holding the student fixed and varying only whether the frozen teacher is the small (124M) or large (1.5B) OWT-pretrained model. We report this comparison at both student scales considered in this work. At both scales, using the larger teacher matches or improves over the smaller one on every domain, indicating that our method continues to benefit from a stronger teacher even though, unlike classical KD, the teacher is never the stronger model at the target task – it is only used as a coarse, high-temperature regularizer (Section 3.2.2).

D.3 Instruction Tuning

Figure 6 reports the full data-availability sweep discussed in Section 4.3, and Figure 7 completes Figure 4 with the four tasks left out of the main paper.

D.4 Baselines for instruction tuning

We compare Ambient SFT with four baselines, each swept over a grid whose best value lies inside the grid:

  • •

    L2-SP (Li et al., 2018) penalizes the distance of the weights from the pre-trained weights. We sweep the penalty strength α∈{0.001,0.01,0.1,1,10}\alpha\in\{0.001,0.01,0.1,1,10\}.

  • •

    NEFTune (Jain et al., 2024) adds uniform noise to the input embeddings during fine-tuning. We sweep the noise scale α∈{5,10,15}\alpha\in\{5,10,15\}.

  • •

    Knowledge distillation (KD) adds to vanilla SFT a KL term to the frozen base model at temperature T=1T=1, i.e., our objective with T=1T=1. We sweep the cross-entropy weight pc∈{0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9}p_{c}\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9\}.

  • •

    Label smoothing mixes the one-hot target with the uniform distribution with weight ϵ\epsilon. We sweep ϵ∈{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4}\epsilon\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4\}.

The best settings are α=10\alpha=10 for NEFTune, α=1\alpha=1 for L2-SP, pc=0.5p_{c}=0.5 for KD and ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2 for label smoothing. Table 22 reports the full sweeps.

D.5 Per-source temperature

Dolci-Instruct-SFT is a mixture of 21 source datasets. For each source ss, we run the base model once over that source’s supervised tokens and measure the gap gsg_{s} between its cross-entropy on the observed tokens and its average predictive entropy. We then raise the temperature where the gap is large, so that the student relies less on the base model there. We use the rule

Ts=2.5​(1+max⁡(gs,0)0.1),T_{s}=2.5\,\left(1+\frac{\max(g_{s},0)}{0.1}\right),

which keeps T=2.5T=2.5 for sources the base model fits well. Sources such as math and code get temperatures between 2.52.5 and 3.43.4, while poorly fit ones, such as CoCoNot and WildChat, get up to 10.710.7. This rule is a simple heuristic rather than a tuned choice: we compared three such rules at Qwen3-1.7B, kept this one, and used its constants unchanged at 4B and 8B. Other rules based on the same gap may work better.

D.6 Reasoning

Table 23 evaluates the Vanilla SFT and Ambient SFT reasoning checkpoints of Table 6 on knowledge benchmarks with the few-shot, non-chat specifications of the instruction-tuning harness (Table 17) on the full test sets. Ambient SFT is ahead on all four benchmarks.

Corollary E.1 (Prefixes sampled from the tempered teacher).

Let pT​θ∗​(𝐱)=∏i=1lpT​θ∗​(xi∣𝐱<i)p_{T\theta^{*}}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{l}p_{T\theta^{*}}(x_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i}) be the distribution of text sampled autoregressively at temperature TT, and let μi\mu_{i} be the distribution of its first i−1i-1 tokens. Then

JT(θ)=𝔼𝐱∼pT​θ∗[∑i=1l−logpT​θ(xi∣𝐱<i)]\displaystyle J_{T}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p_{T\theta^{*}}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{l}-\log p_{T\theta}(x_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})\right] (12)

is the tempered cross-entropy on text sampled at temperature TT, every context lies in the support of μi\mu_{i}, and every minimizer of JTJ_{T} matches the teacher at all temperatures on every context.

Proof of Corollary E.1.

Since pT​θ∗​(𝐱)p_{T\theta^{*}}(\mathbf{x}) is the autoregressive product of the tempered conditionals, under 𝐱∼pT​θ∗\mathbf{x}\sim p_{T\theta^{*}} the prefix 𝐱<i\mathbf{x}_{<i} has distribution μi​(𝐱<i)=∏j<ipT​θ∗​(xj∣𝐱<j)\mu_{i}(\mathbf{x}_{<i})=\prod_{j<i}p_{T\theta^{*}}(x_{j}\mid\mathbf{x}_{<j}) and, given the prefix, xi∼pT​θ∗(⋅∣𝐱<i)x_{i}\sim p_{T\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i}). By the tower rule, 𝔼𝐱∼pT​θ∗[−logpT​θ(xi∣𝐱<i)]=𝔼𝐱<i∼μi𝔼xi∼pT​θ∗(⋅∣𝐱<i)[−logpT​θ(xi∣𝐱<i)]\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p_{T\theta^{*}}}[-\log p_{T\theta}(x_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{<i}\sim\mu_{i}}\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim p_{T\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})}[-\log p_{T\theta}(x_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i})], and summing over ii gives Eq. (12) as the instance of Eq. (5) with these μi\mu_{i}. Because each tempered conditional is a softmax, μi​(𝐱<i)>0\mu_{i}(\mathbf{x}_{<i})>0 for every 𝐱<i∈Vi−1\mathbf{x}_{<i}\in V^{i-1}, so every context lies in the support of μi\mu_{i}, and Theorem 3.1(b) gives recovery on every context. ∎

E.2 Proof of Theorem E.2

Theorem E.2 (High-temperature conditional KL convergence).

Fix a context x<ix_{<i} and let Δ⁡(x<i)\Delta(x_{<i}) be the range of the logit gap between the two models,

Δ⁡(x<i)\displaystyle\Delta(x_{<i}) =maxy∈𝒱⁡[gθpost∗​(y∣x<i)−gθpre∗​(y∣x<i)]−miny∈𝒱⁡[gθpost∗​(y∣x<i)−gθpre∗​(y∣x<i)]\displaystyle=\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\big[g_{\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})-g_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})\big]-\min_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\big[g_{\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})-g_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})\big] (13)
=maxy∈𝒱⁡[gθpre∗​(y∣x<i)−gθpost∗​(y∣x<i)]−miny∈𝒱⁡[gθpre∗​(y∣x<i)−gθpost∗​(y∣x<i)]\displaystyle=\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\big[g_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})-g_{\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})\big]-\min_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\big[g_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})-g_{\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})\big] (14)

For every T>0T>0:

DKL(pT​θpost∗(⋅∣x<i)∥pT​θpre∗(⋅∣x<i))≤Δ​(x<i)28​T2.D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\,\middle\|\,p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\right)\leq\frac{\Delta(x_{<i})^{2}}{8T^{2}}.

The same bound holds with the two models interchanged.

Proof.

The KL divergence of interest is

DKL(pT​θpost∗(⋅∣x<i)∥pT​θpre∗(⋅∣x<i))\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\,\middle\|\,p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\right)
=𝔼Y∼pT​θpost∗(⋅∣x<i)[logpT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})}\left[\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}\right].

We will write the KL divergence in a form to which Hoeffding’s lemma can be applied. Before we do this, let us notice the following easy fact:

𝔼Y∼pT​θpost∗(⋅∣x<i)[exp(−logpT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i))]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})}\left[\exp\left(-\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}\right)\right] =∑y∈𝒱pT​θpost∗​(y∣x<i)​pT​θpre∗​(y∣x<i)pT​θpost∗​(y∣x<i)\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}}p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}
=∑y∈𝒱pT​θpre∗​(y∣x<i)=1.\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}}p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})=1.

We claim that this implies the following:

DKL(pT​θpost∗(⋅∣x<i)∥pT​θpre∗(⋅∣x<i))\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\,\middle\|\,p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\right) (15)
=log⁡𝔼⁡[exp⁡(−log⁡pT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i)+𝔼⁡[log⁡pT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i)])].\displaystyle=\log\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(-\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}+\mathbb{E}\left[\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}\right]\right)\right].

Indeed, the RHS of the above equals:

log⁡(𝔼⁡[exp⁡(−log⁡pT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i))]⋅exp⁡(𝔼⁡[log⁡pT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i)]))\displaystyle\log\Bigg(\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(-\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}\right)\right]\cdot\exp\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}\right]\right)\Bigg)
=log⁡(1⋅exp⁡(𝔼⁡[log⁡pT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i)]))\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~=\log\Bigg(1\cdot\exp\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}\right]\right)\Bigg)
=𝔼⁡[log⁡pT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i)].\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~=\mathbb{E}\left[\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}\right].

Recall that Hoeffding’s lemma implies that, for any random variable ZZ supported on an interval [a,b][a,b],

log⁡𝔼⁡[exp⁡(Z−𝔼⁡[Z])]≤(b−a)28.\log\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z]\right)\right]\leq\frac{(b-a)^{2}}{8}.

We apply Hoeffding’s lemma to the random variable

Z:=−log⁡pT​θpost∗​(Y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(Y∣x<i).Z:=-\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(Y\mid x_{<i})}.

This random variable is bounded because the vocabulary is finite and all logits are finite. Its centered exponential moment is exactly the right-hand side of (15). Therefore,

DKL(pT​θpost∗(⋅∣x<i)∥pT​θpre∗(⋅∣x<i))\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\,\middle\|\,p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\right) (16)
≤18​(maxy∈𝒱⁡log⁡pT​θpost∗​(y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(y∣x<i)−miny∈𝒱⁡log⁡pT​θpost∗​(y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(y∣x<i))2,\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{8}\left(\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}-\min_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}\right)^{2},

where we used the fact that negating a random variable does not change the length of its range.

By the definition of temperature scaling,

log⁡pT​θpost∗​(y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(y∣x<i)\displaystyle\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})} =gθpost∗​(y∣x<i)−gθpre∗​(y∣x<i)T\displaystyle=\frac{g_{\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})-g_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}{T}
+log⁡∑z∈𝒱exp⁡(gθpre∗​(z∣x<i)/T)∑z∈𝒱exp⁡(gθpost∗​(z∣x<i)/T).\displaystyle+\log\frac{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{V}}\exp\!\left(g_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(z\mid x_{<i})/T\right)}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{V}}\exp\!\left(g_{\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(z\mid x_{<i})/T\right)}.

The second term is independent of yy and therefore cancels when taking the difference between the maximum and minimum over tokens. Consequently,

maxy∈𝒱⁡log⁡pT​θpost∗​(y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(y∣x<i)−miny∈𝒱⁡log⁡pT​θpost∗​(y∣x<i)pT​θpre∗​(y∣x<i)\displaystyle\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}-\min_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\log\frac{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}{p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(y\mid x_{<i})}
=Δ⁡(x<i)T.\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta(x_{<i})}{T}.

Substituting this identity into (16) gives

DKL(pT​θpost∗(⋅∣x<i)∥pT​θpre∗(⋅∣x<i))≤Δ​(x<i)28​T2.D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{post}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\,\middle\|\,p_{T\theta_{\mathrm{pre}}^{*}}(\cdot\mid x_{<i})\right)\leq\frac{\Delta(x_{<i})^{2}}{8T^{2}}.

∎

The non-degeneracy condition of Theorem 3.2.

Assume in addition that B≠0B\neq 0 and that (A2) D:=∂THT|T=1D:=\partial_{T}H_{T}|_{T=1} is not a multiple of FF. Throughout, Φ∈ℝ|V|×d\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times d} stacks the token embeddings ϕ​(z)⊤\phi(z)^{\top}, so that Λ⁡(η)=lse⁡(Φ​η)\Lambda(\eta)=\operatorname{lse}(\Phi\eta) with lse(u)=log∑zeuz\operatorname{lse}(u)=\log\sum_{z}e^{u_{z}}, ∇Λ​(η)=Φ⊤​σ​(Φ​η)=μ⁡(η)\nabla\Lambda(\eta)=\Phi^{\top}\sigma(\Phi\eta)=\mu(\eta) and ∇2Λ​(η)=Φ⊤​Σ​(σ⁡(Φ​η))​Φ=Σ⁡(η)\nabla^{2}\Lambda(\eta)=\Phi^{\top}\Sigma(\sigma(\Phi\eta))\Phi=\Sigma(\eta), where σ\sigma is the softmax and Σ⁡(p)=diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤\Sigma(p)=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}. For every λ>0\lambda>0 and T>0T>0:

Remark E.8 (The infimum need not be attained).

Theorem 3.2 asserts a strict inequality, not the existence of a best (λ,T)(\lambda,T), and the distinction is real. The risk depends on the pair only through M=λ​HTM=\lambda H_{T}, so λ\lambda sets the scale of the penalty and TT its shape, and the reachable shapes trace the curve T↦T2​HTT\mapsto T^{2}H_{T}, which starts at FF at T=1T=1 and tends to Σ0⊗G\Sigma_{0}\otimes G as T→∞T\to\infty. Convergence by itself decides nothing about attainment: if the target conditionals are uniform then T2​HT=Σ0⊗GT^{2}H_{T}=\Sigma_{0}\otimes G at every temperature and the curve is a single point. But the limiting shape need not be reachable at any finite TT, and then the joint infimum can fail to be attained even under the non-degeneracy condition. The following example does that, on an open set of teacher gaps. Keep the model of Remark E.7 but take b12=2/nb_{1}^{2}=2/n and b22=1/nb_{2}^{2}=1/n. By the Example below the best penalty eigenvalues are mj∗=1/(n​bj2)m_{j}^{*}=1/(nb_{j}^{2}), that is (12,1)(\tfrac{1}{2},1), whereas the reachable ratio is m1/m2=κ1​(T)/κ2​(T)=cosh2⁡(1/T)m_{1}/m_{2}=\kappa_{1}(T)/\kappa_{2}(T)=\cosh^{2}(1/T), which exceeds 11 at every finite TT and tends to 11 only as T→∞T\to\infty. With λ\lambda free to set the scale, the reachable set is therefore exactly the open cone {m1>m2>0}\{m_{1}>m_{2}>0\}, and the unconstrained optimum (12,1)(\tfrac{1}{2},1) lies outside it. The optimum over the closure is a different point: each coordinate contributes (mj2​bj2+μj/n)/(μj+mj)2(m_{j}^{2}b_{j}^{2}+\mu_{j}/n)/(\mu_{j}+m_{j})^{2}, strictly decreasing then strictly increasing with minimum at mj∗m_{j}^{*}, so from any feasible m1>m2m_{1}>m_{2} one can move to the diagonal without increasing either contribution, and the constrained minimum sits on the face m1=m2m_{1}=m_{2}. That face is disjoint from the reachable set, so the infimum over finite (λ,T)(\lambda,T) is approached only as T→∞T\to\infty with λ∝T2\lambda\propto T^{2} and is never attained. Note that this is a different limit from the maximum-likelihood one in (10), which sends T→∞T\to\infty at fixed λ\lambda and does kill the penalty. Read positively, a missing minimizer says the model would like the hottest teacher available, with λ\lambda raised to compensate for the flattening.

Dependence within documents. Theorem 3.2 is stated for independent prefixes for clarity, but nothing is lost when the n=n1​ln=n_{1}l tokens come from n1n_{1} independent documents of fixed length ll, which is the situation of (4). Group the score by document, Zk=1l​∑i=1l∇ℓk,i​(θλ∗)Z_{k}=\frac{1}{l}\sum_{i=1}^{l}\nabla\ell_{k,i}(\theta^{*}_{\lambda}). The ZkZ_{k} are i.i.d. across kk, so Lemma E.4 applies with n1→∞n_{1}\to\infty at fixed ll, its empirical-curvature concentration now run on the document-level averages, and with constants that may depend on ll. What has to be rechecked is the covariance. Per document it carries an extra factor of ll, so define the token-normalized quantity Vλtok:=l​Cov⁡(Zk)V^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\lambda}:=l\operatorname{Cov}(Z_{k}); the claim is Vλtok=F+O⁡(‖B‖)V^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\lambda}=F+O(\|B\|), which is what the sandwich needs because 1n1​Cov⁡(Zk)=1n1​l​Vλtok=1n​Vλtok\frac{1}{n_{1}}\operatorname{Cov}(Z_{k})=\frac{1}{n_{1}l}V^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\lambda}=\frac{1}{n}V^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\lambda}. Split the per-token score at θpost∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}} into a clean part (μ⁡(Aθpost∗​ψi)−ϕ⁡(xi))​ψi⊤(\mu(A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}\psi_{i})-\phi(x_{i}))\psi_{i}^{\top} and a teacher part λT​(μ⁡(Aθpost∗​ψiT)−μ⁡(Aθpre∗​ψiT))​ψi⊤\frac{\lambda}{T}\big(\mu(\tfrac{A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}\psi_{i}}{T})-\mu(\tfrac{A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{pre}}}\psi_{i}}{T})\big)\psi_{i}^{\top}. Only the clean part is a martingale difference for the prefix filtration: conditionally on 𝐱<i\mathbf{x}_{<i} the token xix_{i} has mean embedding μ⁡(Aθpost∗​ψi)\mu(A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}\psi_{i}), so clean parts at different positions of the same document are uncorrelated and their covariances add, contributing 1l2​∑i𝔼⁡[Σ⁡(Aθpost∗​ψi)⊗ψi​ψi⊤]=Fl\frac{1}{l^{2}}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}[\Sigma(A_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{post}}}\psi_{i})\otimes\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\top}]=\frac{F}{l} to Cov⁡(Zk)\operatorname{Cov}(Z_{k}), hence FF to VλtokV^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\lambda}, with FF now read as an average over positions. The teacher part is not a martingale difference: it is a deterministic function of ψi\psi_{i} whose conditional mean is generally nonzero, and its within-document correlations do not cancel. They are harmless only because the whole term is O⁡(‖B‖)O(\|B\|), so it adds O⁡(‖B‖2)O(\|B\|^{2}) to Cov⁡(Zk)\operatorname{Cov}(Z_{k}), and the cross term with the clean part adds O⁡(‖B‖)O(\|B\|) there, only pairs j>ij>i surviving since rT​(ψj)r_{T}(\psi_{j}) for j≤ij\leq i is measurable with respect to the prefix at ii. In VλtokV^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\lambda} these become O⁡(l​‖B‖2)O(l\|B\|^{2}) and O⁡(l​‖B‖)O(l\|B\|), both absorbed into Vλtok=F+O⁡(‖B‖)V^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\lambda}=F+O(\|B\|) at fixed ll. We do not claim a version with ll growing with n1n_{1}: there the within-document correlations of the teacher term enter a long-run variance, and a martingale central limit theorem would in any case not supply by itself the second-moment remainder that (9) uses. No repetition of contexts is assumed anywhere.
